topics.title: A pampered dog: the passive voice

learn.hook: Cream cakes, chocolates and extra treats every day: is that love or trouble for a little dog?
points: 'A Triumph of Surgery' by James Herriot, a vet, tells of Tricki Woo, a pet dog over-fed and spoiled by his rich owner, Mrs Pumphrey.
Tricki becomes ill and lazy. The vet takes him to his surgery, gives him no food for two days, and lets him play and run with the other dogs. Tricki recovers fully.
Passive voice puts the receiver of the action first: 'Tricki was fed cream cakes.' Form: be + past participle.
The doer can be added with 'by', or left out when it is unknown or unimportant: 'The dog was taken to the surgery.'
Keep the tense the same: is fed (present), was fed (past), has been fed (present perfect), will be fed (future).

example.q: Passage: Bruno, a spoilt beagle in Bandra, was given jalebis and ice cream every day. Soon he was too fat to climb the stairs. He was taken to the vet, was put on a strict diet, and was made to run in the park. Why does the writer use the passive voice here?
steps: The sentences focus on what happened TO Bruno: was given, was taken, was put, was made.
Who did it (owner, vet) is less important than Bruno's story.
So the passive keeps Bruno as the subject of every sentence.
example.answer: To keep the focus on Bruno, the one receiving the actions, rather than on who did them.

learn.reallife: Notices and news reports use the passive: 'The road will be closed on Sunday', 'Two tigers were spotted in Ranthambore.'

games.title: Active to passive
pairs: The dog is examined by the vet.
Tricki was fed by Mrs Pumphrey.
The boy will walk the dog.
The dog will be walked by the boy.
The cook is baking a cake.
A cake is being baked by the cook.

games.title: Passive voice rules
items: The passive voice uses a form of 'be' + past participle.
e.g. was given, is taken, has been cured.
In the passive, the doer must always be mentioned with 'by'.
The doer is often left out when unknown or unimportant.
'The dog was fed' is in the past tense.
Changing to passive also changes the tense.
The tense stays the same; only the voice changes.
'Tricki was spoiled by Mrs Pumphrey' is in the passive voice.
The receiver, Tricki, is the subject.

quiz.q: Who is Tricki Woo in 'A Triumph of Surgery'?
options: A stray dog in the village
quiz.explain: Tricki Woo is Mrs Pumphrey's pampered little dog.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the pet with a person in the story

options: He catches a cold in the rain
He is over-fed and gets too little exercise
He is bitten by another dog
quiz.explain: Too many rich treats and no exercise make him fat and sick.
quiz.mistake: Assumes a common cause of illness

quiz.q: How does the vet cure Tricki?
options: With a strict diet and plenty of play with other dogs
By sending him to the seaside
quiz.explain: No food for two days, then simple food and exercise with other dogs, cure him.

quiz.q: Change to passive: 'Mrs Pumphrey fed Tricki cream cakes.'
options: Tricki is fed cream cakes by Mrs Pumphrey.
Tricki was feeding cream cakes by Mrs Pumphrey.
Tricki fed cream cakes by Mrs Pumphrey.
Tricki was fed cream cakes by Mrs Pumphrey.
quiz.explain: Past active 'fed' becomes past passive 'was fed'.
quiz.mistake: Changes the tense while changing voice

quiz.q: Change to passive: 'The vet examines the dog.'
options: The dog is examined by the vet.
The dog was examined by the vet.
The dog is examining by the vet.

quiz.q: Change to passive: 'They have taken Bruno to the vet.'
options: Bruno was taken by the vet.
Bruno has been taken to the vet.
Bruno has taken to the vet.
Bruno had been taking to the vet.
quiz.explain: Present perfect passive: has been + past participle; 'they' can be left out.
quiz.mistake: Leaves out 'been' or changes the tense

quiz.q: Passage: Bruno, a spoilt beagle in Bandra, was given jalebis and ice cream every day. Soon he was too fat to climb the stairs. He was taken to the vet, was put on a strict diet, and was made to run in the park. What happened to Bruno at the vet?
options: He was taught to climb stairs
He was put on a strict diet and made to run
He was left at the vet's house
quiz.explain: The last line says he was put on a strict diet and made to run in the park.
quiz.mistake: Picks a detail from before the vet visit

options: Given too much care and comfort; spoiled
quiz.explain: A pampered pet is spoiled with too much attention and treats.
quiz.mistake: Thinks pampered means well looked after in a healthy way

teach.ask: Gappu: My teacher says 'The worm was eaten by Gappu' is passive. Why would anyone talk like that?
teach.praise: Chirp! Passive puts the worm first, using 'was eaten'. It's handy when the receiver matters more!
teach.nudge: In a passive sentence, who comes first: the doer or the receiver? Which verb helper is used?

topics.title: Humour in the story: irony and idioms

learn.hook: A dog is 'cured by surgery' without a single cut. How is that a triumph?
points: The title 'A Triumph of Surgery' is ironic: no operation was done; simple diet and exercise cured Tricki.
The story is told by the vet, James Herriot, with gentle humour about Mrs Pumphrey's over-indulgence.
Humour devices: irony (opposite of what is expected), hyperbole (deliberate exaggeration), and funny contrasts.
Idioms are phrases whose meaning differs from the separate words: 'in the pink of health' = very healthy.
Use idioms sparingly and correctly in writing; they make it lively but must fit the context.

example.q: Mrs Kapoor feeds her pug so many laddoos that 'they could feed a whole wedding'. Which humour device is this?
steps: No one could really feed a whole wedding with one pug's laddoos.
The writer exaggerates on purpose to make us laugh.

learn.reallife: Cartoonists like R.K. Laxman used gentle exaggeration and irony to make readers smile about everyday life.

games.title: Idiom and meaning
pairs: let the cat out of the bag

items.text: After two weeks of exercise, Bruno was in the ___ of health.
The test was a piece of ___.
Don't let the ___ out of the bag about the surprise party.
Riya was over the ___ when she won the quiz.
Dadu is feeling under the ___ today, so he is resting.

quiz.q: Why is the title 'A Triumph of Surgery' humorous?
options: No surgery was done; diet and exercise cured the dog
The vet did a very difficult operation
quiz.explain: The 'triumph' came from simple care, not an operation, which is ironic.
The story is told in the first person by the vet.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the main character with the narrator

quiz.explain: Herriot was a vet who wrote stories about his animal patients.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'surgery' in the title means human surgery

quiz.q: What does 'in the pink of health' mean?
quiz.explain: It is an idiom meaning very healthy.
quiz.mistake: Reads the idiom word by word

quiz.q: What does 'let the cat out of the bag' mean?
quiz.explain: It means to reveal a secret, often accidentally.

quiz.q: 'Mrs Kapoor feeds her pug enough laddoos to feed a whole wedding!' Which device is this?
quiz.explain: It is deliberate exaggeration for effect.
quiz.mistake: Does not recognise exaggeration as a device

quiz.explain: Being over the moon means being delighted.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the idiom is about distance

quiz.q: Which sentence uses an idiom correctly?
options: The maths test was a piece of cake, so I failed it.
I ate a piece of cake test for lunch.
She was a piece of cake when she fell ill.
The maths test was a piece of cake, so I finished early.
quiz.explain: 'A piece of cake' means very easy, which fits finishing early.
quiz.mistake: Uses the idiom in a context that contradicts its meaning

teach.ask: Gappu: The vet didn't do any operation, but the story is called 'A Triumph of Surgery'. Isn't that wrong?
teach.praise: Hee-hee-chirp! The title is ironic: no operation, just diet and exercise. That's the joke!
teach.nudge: Was there really an operation? What actually cured the dog?
